questions.scenario: A platform team uses Claude Code across a large monorepo. They maintain a detailed release runbook: a staged checklist, rollback steps, and three helper scripts. Releases happen a few times per sprint. When they pasted the whole runbook into the project CLAUDE.md, every session — including unrelated coding sessions — paid the context cost, and Claude sometimes wove release steps into ordinary work.
questions.stem: Which approach best makes the runbook available for releases while keeping its context cost near zero the rest of the time?

options.text: Keep the runbook in the project CLAUDE.md but wrap it in XML tags so Claude ignores it unless the task is a release.
Package it as a Skill: a concise SKILL.md with the checklist, the helper scripts in the skill directory, invoked as /release when needed.
Build a custom tool that executes the entire release end-to-end so the runbook never enters the conversation at all.
Expose the three helper scripts as tools on an MCP server and describe the checklist inside those tools' descriptions.

questions.explanation: **Skills are the mechanism for on-demand procedural knowledge.** Through progressive disclosure, only the skill's name and description occupy context until it is invoked, so ordinary sessions pay almost nothing, and the helper scripts ship inside the skill directory. CLAUDE.md is for standards that should apply to *every* session — the exact opposite of an occasional runbook.

whyWrong.A: Tags do not gate loading: CLAUDE.md content is injected into every session regardless of markup, so the context cost and step-bleed remain.
whyWrong.C: Collapses a judgment-heavy, multi-step procedure into one opaque action; the team loses Claude's ability to follow, adapt, and report each step, and the runbook knowledge still has no proper home.
whyWrong.D: MCP servers deliver shared live access, not procedural knowledge; burying a staged checklist inside tool descriptions puts it in the wrong place and adds a component to deploy and maintain.

questions.mindset: Match the mechanism to the gap: on-demand know-how → Skill; always-on standards → CLAUDE.md; live access → tools/MCP.

questions.scenario: A customer-support application retrieves the top five knowledge-base articles with its own search service before every Claude call and passes them as documents in the request. Response quality meets targets. A new architect proposes replacing this with an MCP server that exposes search so Claude can "search agentically," arguing it is more flexible. Leadership asks for the change with the lowest cost and risk.
questions.stem: Given that rule-based retrieval already meets quality targets and no use case requires the model to iterate on searches, which course of action is BEST?

options.text: Build the MCP search server now so the agent can issue follow-up searches whenever it decides more results are needed.
Keep app-side retrieval and also add the MCP server, letting Claude choose whichever retrieval path it prefers per ticket.
Replace app-side retrieval with a custom search tool that the model must call several times per ticket to gather its own articles.
Keep the existing app-side retrieval passing articles as input, and add a search tool only if a concrete need for model-driven iteration emerges.

questions.explanation: **Add mechanisms when a requirement demands them, not for hypothetical flexibility.** The retrieval need is deterministic (fixed top-five), already works, and the stated goals are lowest cost and risk. Start simple and add complexity only when it demonstrably helps — an MCP server here buys unneeded "flexibility" at the price of a new deployable, added latency, and a growing tool context.

whyWrong.A: Every new server must be deployed, secured, and paid for in context and maintenance; flexibility with no demonstrated requirement is pure downside.
whyWrong.B: Combines the costs of both paths and makes behavior unpredictable — the model may bypass a retrieval process that already meets quality targets.
whyWrong.C: Forces the same articles through multiple model-driven turns, raising tokens, latency, and failure surface with no quality gain.

questions.mindset: The simplest design that meets the requirement wins; new mechanisms must be justified by a real need.

questions.scenario: Three product teams each maintain their own copy of HTTP glue code so their Claude applications can create, update, and transition tickets in the corporate issue tracker. When the tracker's workflow changes, each app breaks separately and is patched on its own schedule. The platform group wants one integration, owned and maintained in one place, that current and future Claude apps can all use.
questions.stem: Which approach best meets the requirement?

options.text: Consolidate the operations into one MCP server owned by the platform group, exposing create/update/transition as tools that each application connects to.
Move the HTTP calls into each application's system prompt so Claude issues the REST requests itself through a shell tool.
Publish the glue as a shared library and have each app's Claude write ad-hoc scripts against it at runtime.
Keep one custom tool per application but generate all of them from a shared API spec so the implementations stay in sync.

questions.explanation: **An MCP server is the mechanism for access that is shared across applications and maintained independently.** One owner fixes the tracker integration once, authentication and behavior are consistent for every consumer, and new apps connect rather than re-implement. This is exactly the reuse-and-independent-maintenance tradeoff that separates MCP servers from per-app custom tools.

whyWrong.B: Describing access in prompts and executing it through a generic shell tool is fragile, pushes credentials toward the model, and makes every app re-implement the behavior differently.
whyWrong.C: Runtime, model-authored integration code is unreliable and unauditable; the model would re-derive API usage on every run.
whyWrong.D: Generated duplicates are still three deployments to patch; a shared spec reduces but does not remove per-app maintenance and drift.

questions.mindset: When several apps need the same live access and one team should own it, that access belongs behind an MCP server.

questions.scenario: An interactive internal tool calls Claude on behalf of signed-in employees. One capability must execute actions against an internal approvals API using the employee's short-lived session credentials, which live in the application's memory and must not be persisted or forwarded anywhere else. The action must add as little latency as possible, and no other application will ever use this capability.
questions.stem: Which implementation choice best fits these constraints?

options.text: An MCP server that receives the employee token on each call and forwards it to the approvals API on the agent's behalf.
A Skill documenting the approvals API and instructing Claude to call it through Bash using the employee's token.
A custom tool implemented inside the application that uses the in-memory session credentials directly and executes the call in-process.
An MCP server deployed beside the app that stores per-employee tokens in a vault so they can be reused across calls.

questions.explanation: **A custom tool fits app-specific access used by one application.** It runs in the app's process, uses the session credential where it already lives, and adds no network hop. MCP's benefits — cross-app reuse and independent maintenance — are explicitly not needed here, while its costs (a separate deployable, credential hand-off) directly conflict with the constraints. Credentials belong in the harness, never in model-visible text.

whyWrong.A: Every call forwards a credential to another component — the exact pattern the constraint forbids — and adds a hop against the latency budget.
whyWrong.B: A Skill adds know-how, not access: it would route the token through model-visible commands and turn a security boundary into prompt guidance.
whyWrong.D: Persisting short-lived credentials in a vault violates the constraint, and the reuse it enables is explicitly out of scope.

questions.mindset: Single consumer plus tight coupling to app state and secrets → custom tool in the harness, not a standalone server.

questions.scenario: During an architecture review, a team sorts proposed capabilities by the mechanism that should deliver each one: a built-in tool, a custom tool, a Skill, or an MCP server.
questions.stem: For which TWO capabilities is an MCP server the most appropriate primary mechanism? Choose TWO.

options.text: A deployment-status service owned by the platform group that several Claude applications and coding agents must query, maintained independently of any one app.
A pricing calculator that reads one application's in-memory cart state and is meaningless outside that application.
A 30-step incident-response procedure with helper scripts that agents should follow only during incidents.
Governed access to a payments sandbox — centralized authentication, per-call authorization, rate limits, and audit logging — required by multiple teams' agents.
Retrieving current web pages and searching the public web from any Claude application.

questions.explanation: **MCP servers earn their cost when access is shared and independently owned or governed.** A fits the core reuse pattern (multiple consumers, one maintaining owner); D fits the governance pattern, where the server is the natural place to centralize authentication, per-call authorization, rate limits, and audit logs.

whyWrong.B: A single consumer coupled to in-process app state is the textbook custom tool; a server adds infrastructure with no reuse.
whyWrong.C: Procedural knowledge used occasionally is a Skill — progressive disclosure keeps its cost near zero until invoked.
whyWrong.E: Web search and fetch are built-in capabilities that are already maintained and tested; rebuilding them duplicates work for no new ability.

questions.mindset: MCP = shared access with independent ownership or centralized control; everything else maps to tool, Skill, or built-in.

questions.scenario: A team's release-engineering SKILL.md has grown to about 900 lines: the core procedure plus full reference tables, migration examples, and edge cases, all inline. Engineers report that Claude sometimes loses its place mid-procedure, and sessions that invoke the skill consume far more context than expected. The skill otherwise works, and they want a minimal, low-risk fix.

options.text: Move the reference tables and examples into the project CLAUDE.md so the skill itself stays short.
Trim SKILL.md to the core procedure and move tables, examples, and edge cases into supporting files in the skill directory, read only when needed.
Split the skill into three sequential skills — lookup, migrate, verify — that engineers invoke in order during a release.
Serve the reference tables from a new MCP server's resources so the skill becomes a thin index that points at the server.

questions.explanation: **Progressive disclosure works in layers: name and description until invoked, then a concise SKILL.md that points to supporting files loaded on demand.** Guidance is to keep SKILL.md short (under about 500 lines) and push detail into reference files and scripts inside the skill. This preserves one invokable procedure while shrinking what any single session must hold.

whyWrong.A: CLAUDE.md loads in every session for everyone — the cost moves from skill users to all users and gets worse.
whyWrong.C: Sequential skills add human orchestration and multiply discovery surfaces without reducing the total content Claude must read.
whyWrong.D: Static, repo-local reference material does not need a deployed server; this adds a component and a failure mode for zero reuse benefit.

questions.mindset: Skills should stay lean at the top and defer detail to files the model reads only when the task requires it.

questions.scenario: A developer is prototyping a research assistant and has started scaffolding a custom tool: a wrapper around a third-party search API, complete with an API key, retry logic, and a hand-written description. The assistant merely needs current information from the public web from time to time.

options.text: Stop building the wrapper and use the built-in web search and fetch tools, which already provide this capability.
Finish the custom tool — a hand-tuned description will make it more reliable for this assistant than the built-in.
Wrap the search API in an MCP server instead, so the capability is reusable by other applications later.
Skip tools entirely and teach the model, through prompt instructions, to call the search API with Bash curl when it needs facts.

questions.explanation: **Check built-ins first: never rebuild a capability the platform already provides.** Web search and fetch are maintained, tested built-in capabilities whose results Claude already knows how to use. Custom tools and MCP servers are for gaps built-ins cannot fill.

whyWrong.B: Duplicates a maintained capability and inherits keys, rate limits, retries, and description tuning for no new ability.
whyWrong.C: Compounds the same mistake with a deployable component, justified by reuse that may never materialize.
whyWrong.D: Puts an API key within reach of model-issued shell commands and converts a solved capability into fragile prompting.

questions.mindset: Built-in covers it → use the built-in; save custom tooling for real gaps.

questions.scenario: An operations agent built on the Claude Agent SDK has shell and SQL tools for database maintenance. Security policy is absolute: no destructive statement (DROP, TRUNCATE, unbounded DELETE) may run against production without a recorded human approval, no matter how the task is phrased. The team is deciding where that rule should live.
questions.stem: Which mechanism MOST reliably enforces this policy?

options.text: Add the rule as a mandatory first step in the maintenance Skill the agent follows for production work.
State the rule in the system prompt and require the agent to confirm in its answer that it checked before every statement.
Enforce it in code: a PreToolUse hook or permission rule intercepts matching statements, blocks them, and requires recorded human approval.
Route production tasks to the most instruction-following model available and keep the rule in that model's prompt.

questions.explanation: **Must-always and must-never rules need deterministic enforcement in code, not wording.** Prompt-level guidance — Skills, system prompts, self-checks — has a non-zero failure rate; a hook or permission gate runs on every matching call regardless of what the model believes. Skills carry know-how; guarantees belong to the harness.

whyWrong.A: A Skill is guidance loaded into context: it shapes behavior but cannot guarantee it, and this policy tolerates zero exceptions.
whyWrong.B: Self-checking delegates enforcement to the least reliable component — the model judging its own compliance.
whyWrong.D: A stronger instruction-follower still fails occasionally; reliability of wording is not enforcement.

questions.mindset: If the rule admits no exceptions, it belongs in a hook, permission rule, or code gate — never in a prompt.

questions.scenario: A design review produced a list of claims about how Skills fit into an agent's toolchain alongside tools and MCP servers.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements accurately describe Skills? Choose TWO.

options.text: A Skill grants the agent system access or privileges it would not otherwise have.
Until a Skill is invoked, only its name and description occupy context.
Skills are the recommended place for rules that must hold without exception.
Once a Skill exceeds one page, it must be re-implemented as an MCP server.
A Skill packages procedural knowledge and optional helper scripts for on-demand use.

questions.explanation: **Skills add know-how, not access.** They package procedures (and optional scripts) that load on demand (E), and progressive disclosure means only the name and description sit in context until invocation (B). Access and enforcement live elsewhere — in tools/MCP servers and in code-level controls.

whyWrong.A: The defining limitation of Skills: they carry instructions and scripts, not new system access or privileges — access comes from tools and servers.
whyWrong.C: Rules that must always hold need deterministic controls (hooks, permissions, code gates); Skills are probabilistic guidance.
whyWrong.D: Invented rule; long skills are fixed by trimming SKILL.md and deferring detail to supporting files, not by re-platforming.

questions.mindset: Skills = on-demand knowledge with near-zero idle cost; they are neither access nor enforcement.

questions.scenario: A data team wrote a Claude Code Skill that walks Claude through querying the company warehouse with psql over Bash. Results are inconsistent: Claude lacks personal credentials, improvises connection strings, and on one occasion pasted a teammate's token into the transcript. The procedure in the SKILL.md itself is accurate and well written.
questions.stem: What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Add more few-shot psql examples to the SKILL.md so Claude constructs connection strings and commands correctly.
Store a shared service credential in the skill's directory and instruct Claude to read it when connecting.
Grant the local shell profile broader read access to the warehouse so psql connects without per-user setup.
Keep the Skill for procedure and add a governed query tool (custom tool or MCP server) that holds the credentials and runs validated read-only queries.

questions.explanation: **Diagnose the gap before choosing the mechanism: this failure is access, not knowledge.** The procedure is already correct, so more instructions cannot fix missing credentials or unsafe execution. Skills add know-how, not system access — access belongs in a tool or server where credentials live in configuration, inputs are validated, and results return as tool results.

whyWrong.A: More examples polish knowledge that is not the problem; they do nothing about credentials or unsafe execution paths.
whyWrong.B: Places a secret where the model — and the transcript — can read it, institutionalizing the exact incident that occurred.
whyWrong.C: Widens what any model-issued command can reach, increasing blast radius instead of containing it.

questions.mindset: Classify the gap first — knowledge gaps go to Skills, access gaps go to tools or servers.

questions.scenario: A team wants Claude Code and one internal application to work with their issue tracker: search issues, comment, and transition states. A widely used, actively maintained MCP server for that tracker already exists, and their security review has approved it for internal use. A developer nonetheless proposes writing a bespoke server "for full control," estimating a few weeks of effort.
questions.stem: Which course of action is BEST, proportionate to the need?

options.text: Connect the reviewed, maintained MCP server now, and build custom tooling only for workflows it cannot cover.
Build the bespoke server first so the team owns every line, keeping the existing server as a fallback.
Write a Skill that drives the tracker's REST API through curl so no server component is needed at all.
Embed one custom tool per tracker operation in the internal app and have Claude Code call the tracker's CLI through Bash.

questions.explanation: **Proportionate design reuses existing, maintained servers and reserves custom MCP development for workflows the ecosystem does not cover.** The approved server already handles auth, quirks, and upstream changes; the team's remaining effort should go to genuinely team-specific gaps.

whyWrong.B: "Full control" buys duplicated maintenance and slower fixes for capability that already exists and passed review.
whyWrong.C: Conflates knowledge with access: driving a REST API through curl pushes authentication into model-issued commands and re-derives API behavior every run.
whyWrong.D: Maintains two divergent integrations and leans on raw shell access for the coding side — more glue, more drift, more risk.

questions.mindset: Reuse built-ins and existing servers first; build custom only where a real gap remains.

questions.scenario: A support team added an incident-triage Skill to their Claude Code setup. The SKILL.md body is thorough, but Claude almost never starts it on its own during incidents; engineers have to invoke /triage manually. They want Claude to recognize incident work and pull the procedure in by itself.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Move the skill's full contents into CLAUDE.md so every session sees the procedure and cannot miss it.
Convert the procedure into a custom tool so it sits in the tools array, where Claude always sees its name.
Disable every other skill so triage is the only one Claude can select when incident work arrives.
Rewrite the skill's description and when-to-use text so the listing names its triggers — alerts, degraded services, incident channels.

questions.explanation: **Skill discovery runs on the listing, not the body.** Only the name and description occupy context before invocation, so however good the SKILL.md is, the model can only select the skill if the listing says when it applies. Fixing the description and when-to-use guidance directly addresses why automatic invocation never fires.

whyWrong.A: Pays the full context cost in every session and still does not teach selective, criteria-based use.
whyWrong.B: A multi-step procedure is not an action with a schema; disguising it as a callable tool distorts it and bloats the tool list.
whyWrong.C: Removing other skills damages unrelated workflows and does nothing to make the triage listing more informative.

questions.mindset: If a skill is never auto-invoked, the listing is the problem — the body is invisible until after selection.

questions.scenario: An internal release-management assistant needs three capabilities: live read access to the deployment service, which the platform group already exposes as an MCP server used by two other applications; a 40-step rollback procedure used only during incidents; and occasional lookups in public vendor documentation.
questions.stem: Which design BEST assigns each need to the right mechanism?

options.text: One new MCP server that exposes deployment tools, serves the rollback procedure as a prompt template, and adds its own web-search tool.
Custom tools inside the app for all three: deployment reads, a rollback_steps tool, and a hand-built documentation search.
Connect the platform group's MCP server for deployment access, package the rollback procedure as a Skill, and use built-in web tools for documentation.
Put the rollback procedure in the system prompt, call the deployment service through Bash curl, and skip documentation lookups entirely.

questions.explanation: **Strong designs combine mechanisms, each doing what it does best: MCP for shared live access, a Skill for on-demand procedural knowledge, built-ins for generic actions.** This reuses the existing server, keeps the 40-step procedure out of context until an incident, and avoids rebuilding public-web capability.

whyWrong.A: Forces one mechanism onto every need: procedures do not belong in a server, it duplicates access that already exists, and adding a web-search tool rebuilds a maintained built-in.
whyWrong.B: Single-app tools surrender the reuse the platform group already provides, and the hand-built search duplicates a built-in.
whyWrong.D: An always-loaded 40-step procedure bloats every request, curl pushes service credentials toward model-issued commands, and a stated need goes unmet.

questions.mindset: Assign each requirement to the mechanism whose strengths match it — access, knowledge, or generic action.

questions.scenario: A team is building a customer-support agent with the Claude Agent SDK. Two needs are confirmed: agents must pull live order status from a service owned by the orders team (a second application will need the same access next quarter), and agents must follow a long escalation procedure that applies only when escalation criteria are met. Generic web access is not required.
questions.stem: Which TWO additions best cover the confirmed needs? Choose TWO.

options.text: Inline the full escalation procedure into the system prompt of every request so it is always present.
Add a hand-built web-search tool so agents can look up policy pages when needed.
Package the escalation procedure as a Skill the agent invokes when the criteria appear.
Have the agent signal "needs order data" with a special phrase that the harness string-matches.
Give agents an order-status tool via the orders team's MCP server (or a custom tool until reuse lands).

questions.explanation: **Each confirmed need maps to one mechanism.** Live access to an internal service → a tool, delivered through the orders team's MCP server since a second consumer is coming; conditional procedural knowledge → a Skill whose content loads only when escalation criteria appear.

whyWrong.A: Pays the procedure's full context cost on every request, escalation or not, and still gives no live order access.
whyWrong.B: Adds an unneeded capability that duplicates a maintained built-in — scope creep, not a confirmed need.
whyWrong.D: Parsing natural-language signals to trigger behavior is a known anti-pattern; the model should request data through actual tool calls.

questions.mindset: Access → tool/MCP; conditional procedure → Skill; never invent unrequested capabilities.

questions.scenario: While reviewing a design document, a team classifies each proposed capability as either a custom tool implemented inside their application or a standalone MCP server.
questions.stem: For which TWO capabilities is a custom tool the more appropriate choice? Choose TWO.

options.text: A discount estimator that reads the application's in-memory cart state and will not be used by any other consumer.
An inventory lookup that the supply-chain group must expose to four other teams' agents with centralized permissions.
A thin wrapper around an internal library call that only this application's agent makes, with no reuse on the roadmap.
A collection of standard-operating-procedure documents that auditors want agents to consult during reviews.
Reading and editing repository files for a coding agent that already ships with built-in file tools.

questions.explanation: **A custom tool fits app-specific access with a single consumer: it runs in the app's process, uses app state directly, and adds nothing to deploy.** A (coupled to in-memory state) and C (single caller, no reuse planned) are exactly that case. MCP earns its overhead only when multiple consumers, independent maintenance, or centralized governance are in play.

whyWrong.B: Four consumer teams, a distinct owner, and centralized permissions are the MCP server pattern, not a per-app tool.
whyWrong.D: Static reference material is knowledge to load on demand — skill support files or server resources — not an action to execute in app code.
whyWrong.E: Duplicating built-in file tools rebuilds a maintained capability the agent already has.

questions.mindset: Single consumer plus app-internal coupling → custom tool; shared, governed, or maintained independently → MCP.
